summary: Nora now keeps what the group has established — not just what was said — and can search it when a question needs more than the last few messages.
details: She notices claims worth keeping in ordinary conversation, checks them, and keeps the ones that hold up with a note of who said it and what backs it. Nothing about a person in the room is kept: that is refused at the point of writing and counted, not filtered later.

A handful of what she holds about whatever is being discussed rides in front of every message, along with a line saying how many more there are — so that reaching for the rest is an obvious thing to do rather than a guess.

Asking her a question she cannot answer from the conversation now searches what she holds. It searches by meaning as well as by words and across languages, so a question in Cantonese finds something written in English and the other way round.

When somebody tells her she has something wrong, the claim is marked as disputed rather than deleted — it keeps appearing, marked, with who objected and what they said. One person's objection does not remove something true for everyone.
A claim she has replaced stops being findable, and a disputed one comes back marked, on the search path as well as in the block. What she shows and what she searches agree.
limitations: Two of the three retrieval channels are built. Traversal — 'what else is connected to this' — is not, so she finds things that MENTION what you asked about and not yet things merely related to it.
Every search pays for the cross-language step even when an exact name match already settled it. That is cost, not correctness, and it is measured.

Names are matched exactly. Two spellings of one thing stay two things until something merges them, which is deliberate: wrongly keeping them apart is a missing connection, and wrongly merging them corrupts both.
